Title: Inline Skating Downhill: Trust One Stop on the Flat Before Any Hill
Description: A certified coach's entry condition for slope practice is stricter than it sounds: at least one fluent stop on the flat that already stops you from your top speed. Not one you are learning — one you trust. Until then, stay on flat ground. And a hill I doubt I can stop on, I ride it out rather than brake — Cass. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: Why the Powerslide Beats a T-Stop on a Hill
Description: On a slope, a certified coach rates the powerslide as by far the most effective stop of those relying on technique rather than hardware: it stops you at a precise point, and it does not strain your muscles the way a T-stop does when held against a gradient. Precision and no strain are the two things a hill takes from you. Steeper than my stops? I ride it out — Cass. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: The Powerslide Takes Months of Practice, Not Sessions
Description: It is learnable, including from a forward transition entry — but a certified coach is blunt about the timescale: it takes several months of conscious practice to build up the entry speed enough for the powerslide to be useful in a real situation. Knowing the shape of it is not the same as owning it at speed. A hill past what I own, I ride it out — Cass. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Heel Brake on a Hill: Sit Down and Push It Forward
Description: A certified coach's downhill heel brake: scissor the braking foot forward, most of your weight on the back supporting leg, apply and release as needed. To finish, sit down into a deep support-leg knee bend and push the brake past your front wheels. Mine was never powerful enough to stop me and hurt my shin, so I took it off, and a hill I doubt I can stop on I ride it out — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: Downhill Plough: Your Knees Must Cover Your Toes
Description: A student's plough looked right on a real slope and scrubbed no speed at all. The fault was knee bend: from a side view her kneecaps did not cover her toes. Bend until they do, and your legs become shock absorbers that press the edges into the road and take speed out at every step. Straight legs cannot absorb a gradient. A hill I doubt I can stop on, I ride it out — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: stepping plough downhill, knee bend skating, inline skating posture, how to slow down on a hill

Title: Turn Your Toes In Further With Every Single Step
Description: On a hill, a fixed toe angle is why a plough feels like it does nothing. A certified coach's progression: start each stop around 20 to 30 degrees of toe-in, and increase it with every step until you are near 45 at the last one. Sharp inversion plus a low knee bend is what makes stopping force on a steep slope. A hill past that, I ride it out instead — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: Going Through the Motions Is Not Stopping
Description: Filmed on a real slope, a student stepped correctly the whole way down and never slowed. That is the trap of the stepping plough: the shape of the movement is easy, and the shape alone brakes nothing. Speed comes off two ways only — knees deep enough to load the edges, and toes turning further in at each step. Past my stops, I ride it out — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: Downhill T-Stop: 80% of You on the Front Leg
Description: A certified coach's downhill T-stop, by weight: 80% or more on the front supporting leg, that knee deeply bent, riding a centre edge. The back skate stays light and narrow and drags behind you to control speed — it is not where your weight lives. Finish by pulling the back foot firmly in while the front knee sinks deeper. Steeper than that, I ride it out — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: If Your Sliding Skate Grips, It Is Carrying Too Much
Description: The powerslide, then its one diagnostic. Start in a scissor, transition backward, slide the front leg out in front of you, and lower your chest toward your thighs so all your weight moves onto the support leg. If the sliding skate grips instead of sliding, it is too heavy: the fix is not the sliding foot, it is bending the support knee deeper. Beyond that, I ride it out — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: powerslide technique, sliding skate grips, inline skate emergency stop, rollerblade powerslide

Title: Don't Skip the Lunge Turn on the Way to a Powerstop
Description: The shortcut to a powerstop is landing on your hip a thousand times. A certified coach's order is the lunge turn, then the lunge stop, then the powerstop — and the first two are not stepping stones, they are useful stops in their own right that you will actually use. Skipping them is how the powerstop stays a fall with a name. Hills past my stops, I ride it out — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
